items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A high-energy photon emitted when a nucleus drops from an excited state to a lower energy state"?
items.answer: gamma ray
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of gamma ray.

items.stem: A student in Bogotá is checking notes on alpha, beta and gamma decay and nuclear equations. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Nuclear power contributes a tiny fraction (<0.1 %); radon, rocks, cosmic rays, food and medical uses dominate.
The whole sample never decays completely in a finite time; the half-life is the time for the number of nuclei to halve.
Stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon: Fe-56 ≈ 8.8 MeV vs U-238 ≈ 7.6 MeV.
In alpha decay the nucleon number decreases by 2.
items.answer: In alpha decay the nucleon number decreases by 2.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: It decreases by 4 (two protons and two neutrons); the proton number decreases by 2.

items.stem: Distinguish between β⁻ decay and β⁺ decay.
items.answer: β⁻: a neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino (Z increases by 1); β⁺: a proton becomes a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino (Z decreases by 1). A is unchanged in both.
items.markingKey: β⁻: a neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino (Z increases by 1); β⁺: a proton becomes a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino (Z decreases by 1). A is unchanged in both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A beta-minus particle is an electron that was orbiting the atom." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The β⁻ electron is created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton; it is not an orbital electron.
items.markingKey: The β⁻ electron is created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton; it is not an orbital electron. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A decay chain starts at ²³⁹Pu (Z = 94) and ends at a nuclide with Z = 96 and A = 231. Determine the number of α and β⁻ decays in the chain.
items.answer: 2 α and 6 β⁻
items.markingKey: A changes only in α decay: (239 − 231)/4 = 2 α (M1 A1); Z: 94 − 2×2 + n_β = 96 → n_β = 6 (M1 A1).

items.stem: ⁹⁰Sr (Z = 38) undergoes β⁻ decay. What are the proton number and nucleon number of the daughter?
items.markingKey: B. β⁻ decay: Z + 1, A unchanged.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The neutrino was accepted by physicists as soon as Pauli proposed it."
items.answer: Acceptance was gradual; the hypothesis was supported by theory (Fermi) and later confirmed by detection – an example of a prediction preceding evidence (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it rescued energy and momentum conservation in beta decay. Arguments against: Pauli himself called it a "desperate remedy"; some (e.g. Bohr) considered abandoning conservation of energy; it was not detected until Cowan and Reines in 1956. Supported judgement: Acceptance was gradual; the hypothesis was supported by theory (Fermi) and later confirmed by detection – an example of a prediction preceding evidence (NOS).

items.stem: Potassium-40 (Z = 19) can decay either by β⁻ emission (89 %) or by electron capture (11 %). (a) Write equations for both decays. (b) Explain why the β⁻ electrons have a continuous energy spectrum while the electron-capture neutrinos have a single energy. (c) Explain how this decay is used to date volcanic rocks (the K–Ar method).
items.answer: (a) ⁴⁰₁₉K → ⁴⁰₂₀Ca + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ; ⁴⁰₁₉K + ⁰₋₁e → ⁴⁰₁₈Ar + νₑ; (b) three products share the energy in β⁻ decay, two (Ar recoil and neutrino) in capture, so the neutrino energy is fixed; (c) argon gas escapes molten lava but is trapped once rock solidifies; the ratio of ⁴⁰Ar to ⁴⁰K, with the known half-life (1.25 × 10⁹ y) and branching ratio, gives the time since solidification.
items.markingKey: Both equations balanced (A1 A1); three-body vs two-body argument (R1); argon trapped after solidification (R1); age from ratio and half-life (R1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "beta-plus decay".
items.answer: The decay of a proton in the nucleus into a neutron, a positron (emitted) and an electron neutrino
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the decay of a proton in the nucleus into a neutron, a positron (emitted) and an electron neutrino. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why charge and nucleon number are conserved in nuclear equations, and how this helps to balance them.
items.answer: Charge and baryon (nucleon) number are conserved in all nuclear reactions, so the totals of Z and A must be equal on both sides; unknown products are found from the differences.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Charge and baryon (nucleon) number are conserved in all nuclear reactions, so the totals of Z and A must be equal on both sides; unknown products are found from the differences. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which interaction is responsible for beta decay?
items.answer: the weak interaction
items.markingKey: B. Weak force changes quark flavour.

items.stem: ²²⁶Ra (Z = 88) undergoes α decay. What are the proton number and nucleon number of the daughter?
items.markingKey: D. α decay: Z − 2, A − 4.

items.stem: A student claims: "A beta-minus particle is an electron that was orbiting the atom." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The β⁻ electron is created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton; it is not an orbital electron.
items.markingKey: The β⁻ electron is created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton; it is not an orbital electron. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: ²³⁸U (Z = 92) undergoes α decay. What are the proton number and nucleon number of the daughter?
items.markingKey: D. α decay: Z − 2, A − 4.

items.stem: Thorium-232 (Z = 90) decays through a chain to lead-208 (Z = 82). (a) Determine the numbers of α and β⁻ decays. (b) Explain why the chain contains both types of decay. (c) Explain why radon-220, an intermediate member, is a hazard in buildings on granite.
items.answer: (a) ΔA = 24 → 6 α; Z: 90 − 12 + n_β = 82 → 4 β⁻; (b) α decay lowers Z and A but raises N/Z relative to the stability band, so β⁻ decays convert neutrons to protons to return towards stability; (c) radon is a gas that seeps out of the rock and is inhaled; its alpha-emitting daughters lodge in the lungs.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔA = 24 → 6 α; Z: 90 − 12 + n_β = 82 → 4 β⁻; (b) α decay lowers Z and A but raises N/Z relative to the stability band, so β⁻ decays convert neutrons to protons to return towards stability; (c) radon is a gas that seeps out of the rock and is inhaled; its alpha-emitting daughters lodge in the lungs.

items.stem: Define the term "decay constant".
items.answer: The probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay, λ = ln 2/T½
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay, λ = ln 2/T½. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Freya writes four statements while revising half-life and the radioactive decay law. Which one is a misconception?
options: Neutrons are uncharged; they are held by the strong nuclear force.
It decreases by 4 (two protons and two neutrons); the proton number decreases by 2.
Electrons are bound by the electromagnetic force; the strong force does not act on electrons (leptons).
Heating a radioactive source shortens its half-life.
items.answer: Heating a radioactive source shortens its half-life.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Half-life is independent of temperature and chemical state.

items.stem: Distinguish between half-life and decay constant.
items.answer: Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay; the decay constant is the probability per unit time of decay for one nucleus; they are related by λ = ln 2/T½.
items.markingKey: Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay; the decay constant is the probability per unit time of decay for one nucleus; they are related by λ = ln 2/T½. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A sample contains 160 mg of a radioisotope with a half-life of 10 days. What mass of the isotope remains after 30 days?
items.markingKey: A. 3 half-lives: 160/2^3 = 20.0 mg.

items.stem:
The background-corrected count rate C from a short-lived source is recorded every 60 s. Theory: C = C₀e^(−λt).

t / s | C / counts s⁻¹
0 | 931
60 | 648
120 | 446
180 | 325
240 | 224
300 | 165

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the half-life of the source. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State the half-life with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) ln C (y) against t (x); (b) gradient ≈ −0.00579 s⁻¹; (c) 120 s; (d) 120 s ± 6 s
items.markingKey: (a) ln C (y) against t (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ −0.00579 s⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) T½ = ln 2/|gradient| = 120 s (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 5 % of the value = 6 s; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Heating a radioactive source shortens its half-life." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Half-life is independent of temperature and chemical state.
items.markingKey: Half-life is independent of temperature and chemical state. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A patient is injected with technetium-99m (half-life 6.01 h) of activity 400 MBq. (a) Calculate the decay constant in s⁻¹. (b) Calculate the number of Tc-99m nuclei injected. (c) Determine the activity when imaging begins 3 h later. (d) Determine how long it takes for the activity to fall below 1 MBq. (e) Suggest why a gamma emitter with this half-life is suitable.
items.answer: (a) 3.20 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹; (b) 1.25 × 10¹³; (c) 283 MBq; (d) 51.9 h; (e) gamma escapes the body for detection with little ionisation; short half-life limits dose

items.stem: "Radiocarbon dating can be used to date any ancient object." Discuss.
items.answer: Powerful but limited to organic materials younger than about 50 000 years, with calibration; other isotopes are needed for rocks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: excellent for organic material up to ~50 000 years; calibrated against tree rings. Arguments against: only for once-living material containing carbon; too few ¹⁴C nuclei remain after ~10 half-lives; atmospheric ¹⁴C levels have varied (calibration needed); contamination with modern carbon. Supported judgement: Powerful but limited to organic materials younger than about 50 000 years, with calibration; other isotopes are needed for rocks. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "random decay"?
options: One-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻²
The property that it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability of decay in a given time
The time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) of a sample to fall to half its initial value
N/Z, which is about 1 for light stable nuclei and rises to about 1.5 for the heaviest stable nuclei
items.answer: The property that it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability of decay in a given time
items.markingKey: B. "random decay" is the property that it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability of decay in a given time.

items.stem: Two samples of the same isotope have masses 2 g and 8 g. Compared with the small sample, the large sample has
options: the same activity and four times the half-life
four times the activity and the same half-life
items.answer: four times the activity and the same half-life
items.markingKey: D. A = λN; λ fixed for the isotope.

items.stem: Explain why background radiation must be measured and subtracted when determining half-life.
items.answer: The detector also records counts from cosmic rays and natural radioactivity; these do not decay with the sample, so if not subtracted they make the measured count rate fall less steeply, overestimating the half-life.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The detector also records counts from cosmic rays and natural radioactivity; these do not decay with the sample, so if not subtracted they make the measured count rate fall less steeply, overestimating the half-life. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A wooden artefact has a carbon-14 activity per gram that is 60 % of that of living wood. Taking the half-life of carbon-14 as 5730 years, estimate the age of the artefact.
items.answer: 4220 years

items.stem: "The half-life is half the time it takes for the whole sample to decay." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The whole sample never decays completely in a finite time; the half-life is the time for the number of nuclei to halve.
items.markingKey: The whole sample never decays completely in a finite time; the half-life is the time for the number of nuclei to halve. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which nuclide has the highest binding energy per nucleon?
items.answer: Iron-56 (or nickel-62), about 8.8 MeV
items.markingKey: Iron-56 (or nickel-62), about 8.8 MeV (A1). The peak of the curve is near A ≈ 56–62.

items.stem: A nucleus X has a larger total binding energy than nucleus Y. Which statement must be true?
options: X has more binding energy per nucleon
X is more stable than Y
more energy is needed to separate X completely into nucleons
items.answer: more energy is needed to separate X completely into nucleons
items.markingKey: C. Total BE measures complete separation energy; stability needs BE/A.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the binding energy per nucleon curve explains why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy.
items.answer: The curve rises steeply for light nuclei to a peak near iron and falls slowly for heavy nuclei; fusing light nuclei or splitting heavy nuclei both move the products towards the peak, increasing total binding energy and releasing the difference as kinetic energy of the products. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The curve rises steeply for light nuclei to a peak near iron and falls slowly for heavy nuclei; fusing light nuclei or splitting heavy nuclei both move the products towards the peak, increasing total binding energy and releasing the difference as kinetic energy of the products. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The binding energy per nucleon of ⁷Li (Z = 3) is 5.606 MeV. What is its total binding energy?
items.markingKey: C. E_B = A × (E_B/A) = 7 × 5.606 = 39.2 MeV; multiplying by Z or N is a common error.

items.stem: A student claims: "Binding energy is the energy stored in a nucleus that is released when it forms bonds." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Binding energy is the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart; it is released when the nucleus forms, so bound nuclei have LESS energy (mass) than free nucleons.
items.markingKey: Binding energy is the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart; it is released when the nucleus forms, so bound nuclei have LESS energy (mass) than free nucleons. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Einstein’s equation E = mc² explains where the energy in nuclear reactions comes from."
items.answer: E = mc² quantifies the release, while the underlying cause is the change in nuclear binding (strong force); both perspectives are needed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: mass defect × c² gives the energy released accurately. Arguments against: the energy arises from the strong nuclear force doing work as nucleons rearrange; E = mc² is the accounting; mass–energy equivalence applies to chemical reactions too, but the changes are tiny. Supported judgement: E = mc² quantifies the release, while the underlying cause is the change in nuclear binding (strong force); both perspectives are needed.

items.stem: 1 u of mass is equivalent to
items.markingKey: B. From E = mc².

items.stem: A student in Nairobi is checking notes on mass defect, binding energy and binding energy per nucleon. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon: Fe-56 ≈ 8.8 MeV vs U-238 ≈ 7.6 MeV.
Half-life is independent of temperature and chemical state.
It decreases by 4 (two protons and two neutrons); the proton number decreases by 2.
Binding energy is the energy stored in a nucleus that is released when it forms bonds.
items.answer: Binding energy is the energy stored in a nucleus that is released when it forms bonds.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Binding energy is the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart; it is released when the nucleus forms, so bound nuclei have LESS energy (mass) than free nucleons.

items.stem: Explain the difference between binding energy and binding energy per nucleon.
items.answer: Binding energy is the total energy to separate all nucleons of a nucleus; per-nucleon binding energy divides this by A and is the better measure of stability for comparing nuclei.
items.markingKey: Binding energy is the total energy to separate all nucleons of a nucleus; per-nucleon binding energy divides this by A and is the better measure of stability for comparing nuclei. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Calculate the minimum energy in joules needed to separate a ¹⁴N nucleus (binding energy per nucleon 7.476 MeV) into its individual nucleons, and the mass equivalent of this energy.

Consider the fusion reaction ²H + ³H → ⁴He + 1 ¹₀n. Binding energies per nucleon: ²H: 1.112 MeV; ³H: 2.827 MeV; ⁴He: 7.074 MeV (free neutrons have zero binding energy). (a) Calculate the energy released per reaction in MeV. (b) Calculate the energy released per kilogram of reactant. (c) Explain, with reference to the binding-energy curve, why this reaction releases energy.
items.answer: (a) 17.6 MeV; (b) 3.39 × 10¹⁴ J kg⁻¹; (c) products have higher binding energy per nucleon
items.markingKey: (a) total BE of products − reactants (M1) = 28.30 − 10.71 = 17.6 MeV (A1). (b) reactant mass ≈ 5 u = 8.31 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (M1); 2.81 × 10⁻¹² J/8.31 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 3.39 × 10¹⁴ J kg⁻¹ (A1). (c) moves towards the peak near Fe-56 (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The low level of ionising radiation always present, from natural sources (radon, rocks, cosmic rays, food) and artificial sources (medical, fallout)"?
items.answer: background radiation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of background radiation.

items.stem: Explain why alpha sources are dangerous inside the body but relatively harmless outside it.
items.answer: Outside, alpha particles are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin; inside (inhaled or ingested), all their energy is deposited in a small volume of living tissue, causing intense ionisation and cell damage.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Outside, alpha particles are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin; inside (inhaled or ingested), all their energy is deposited in a small volume of living tissue, causing intense ionisation and cell damage. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Gamma rays are completely stopped by a thin sheet of lead." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Gamma intensity decreases gradually (exponentially) with thickness; even several cm of lead only reduce it by a large factor.
items.markingKey: Gamma intensity decreases gradually (exponentially) with thickness; even several cm of lead only reduce it by a large factor. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Gamma rays from a source are absorbed by lead with a half-value thickness of 0.866 cm. Calculate the fraction of the gamma intensity transmitted through 1 cm of lead.

A Geiger–Müller tube records 54 counts per minute with no source present. A beta source is placed 4.0 cm away and the count rate rises to 1254 counts per minute. (a) Determine the corrected count rate. (b) An aluminium sheet of thickness 2.0 mm reduces the measured rate to 354 counts per minute; calculate the fraction of beta particles transmitted. (c) Explain why the uncertainty in the count rate is larger when the counts are low.
items.answer: (a) 1200 counts per minute; (b) (354 − 54)/1200 = 0.25; (c) radioactive counts fluctuate randomly with uncertainty ≈ √N, so the fractional uncertainty 1/√N is larger for small N.
items.markingKey: (a) 1200 counts per minute; (b) (354 − 54)/1200 = 0.25; (c) radioactive counts fluctuate randomly with uncertainty ≈ √N, so the fractional uncertainty 1/√N is larger for small N.

items.stem: Freya writes four statements while revising penetration, ionising ability and background radiation. Which one is a misconception?
options: Background radiation comes mainly from nuclear power stations.
Gamma intensity decreases gradually (exponentially) with thickness; even several cm of lead only reduce it by a large factor.
Binding energy is the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart; it is released when the nucleus forms, so bound nuclei have LESS energy (mass) than free nucleons.
Half-life is independent of temperature and chemical state.
items.answer: Background radiation comes mainly from nuclear power stations.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: Nuclear power contributes a tiny fraction (<0.1 %); radon, rocks, cosmic rays, food and medical uses dominate.

items.stem: Explain the difference between alpha radiation and gamma radiation.
items.answer: Alpha: helium nuclei, charge +2e, strongly ionising, stopped by paper/few cm of air; gamma: high-energy photons, uncharged, weakly ionising, reduced significantly only by several cm of lead or metres of concrete.
items.markingKey: Alpha: helium nuclei, charge +2e, strongly ionising, stopped by paper/few cm of air; gamma: high-energy photons, uncharged, weakly ionising, reduced significantly only by several cm of lead or metres of concrete. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A gamma source gives 1600 counts per minute at 10 cm. At 40 cm (corrected for background) the count rate is about
items.answer: 100 counts per minute
items.markingKey: A. Inverse square: 1600/16.

items.stem: "The risk from background radiation is so small that it can be ignored." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For most people the risk is small, but radon in some homes is significant and worth reducing.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: average dose ~2–3 mSv per year, with no clear detectable harm at this level. Arguments against: radon is a leading cause of lung cancer among non-smokers; doses vary widely with location, altitude and occupation (aircrew); linear no-threshold model assumes some risk at any dose. Supported judgement: For most people the risk is small, but radon in some homes is significant and worth reducing. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A short-range (~10⁻¹⁵ m) attractive force between nucleons that holds the nucleus together, repulsive at very short separations (< ~0.5 fm)"?
items.answer: strong nuclear force
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of strong nuclear force.

items.stem: Explain why very heavy nuclei (Z > 83) are all unstable.
items.answer: Electric repulsion acts between every pair of protons (long range, ∝ Z²) while the strong force acts only between neighbouring nucleons; beyond Z ≈ 83 repulsion makes the nucleus unstable, usually decaying by alpha emission.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Electric repulsion acts between every pair of protons (long range, ∝ Z²) while the strong force acts only between neighbouring nucleons; beyond Z ≈ 83 repulsion makes the nucleus unstable, usually decaying by alpha emission. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Neutrons are held in the nucleus by electric attraction to protons." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Neutrons are uncharged; they are held by the strong nuclear force.
items.markingKey: Neutrons are uncharged; they are held by the strong nuclear force. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two protons in a nucleus are 2.0 fm apart. What is the electric force between them?
items.markingKey: A. F = ke²/r² = 57.5 N (repulsive).

items.stem: ⁹⁰Sr has 38 protons and 52 neutrons. Which decay mode is most likely?
items.answer: β⁻
items.markingKey: C. N/Z = 1.37; neutron-rich → β⁻.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The strong nuclear force is the most important of the fundamental forces."
items.answer: Each force dominates at its own scale; "most important" depends on the phenomenon considered.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it binds nuclei and makes atoms and chemistry possible; it is the strongest at nuclear distances. Arguments against: gravity governs planets, stars and galaxies; electromagnetism governs chemistry and materials; the weak force drives stellar fusion (p → n). Supported judgement: Each force dominates at its own scale; "most important" depends on the phenomenon considered.

items.stem: Heavy stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons because
options: extra neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electric repulsion
items.answer: extra neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electric repulsion
items.markingKey: A. Coulomb repulsion grows as Z².

items.stem: Leila writes four statements while revising fundamental forces and the stability of nuclei. Which one is a misconception?
options: Gamma emission does not change Z or A; the element is unchanged.
The strong force holds electrons in their orbits.
Gamma intensity decreases gradually (exponentially) with thickness; even several cm of lead only reduce it by a large factor.

items.answer: The strong force holds electrons in their orbits.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Electrons are bound by the electromagnetic force; the strong force does not act on electrons (leptons).

items.stem: ²³⁸U (Z = 92) is unstable. Calculate its neutron-to-proton ratio, state where it lies relative to the band of stability and predict its likely decay mode.
items.answer: N/Z = 1.59; beyond the end of the band (very heavy); α

items.stem: Two protons in a nucleus are 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart. Calculate the ratio of the electric force to the gravitational force between them, and comment on the role of gravity in nuclear stability.
items.answer: 1.23 × 10³⁶; gravity is negligible
items.markingKey: F_e = 57.5 N, F_g = 4.67 × 10⁻³⁵ N (M1 A1); ratio 1.23 × 10³⁶ – gravity plays no role (R1).

items.stem: Explain, using the forces between nucleons, why (a) the binding energy per nucleon is roughly constant for medium and heavy nuclei, (b) very light nuclei have low binding energy per nucleon, and (c) the curve falls slowly for the heaviest nuclei.
items.answer: (a) The strong force is short-range, so each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours (saturation), giving a roughly constant BE per nucleon; (b) in light nuclei a large fraction of nucleons are at the surface with fewer neighbours; (c) electric repulsion acts between all pairs of protons and grows as Z², reducing BE per nucleon for large Z.
items.markingKey: (a) The strong force is short-range, so each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours (saturation), giving a roughly constant BE per nucleon; (b) in light nuclei a large fraction of nucleons are at the surface with fewer neighbours; (c) electric repulsion acts between all pairs of protons and grows as Z², reducing BE per nucleon for large Z.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "beta-plus decay"?
options: The decay of a neutron in the nucleus into a proton, an electron (emitted) and an electron antineutrino
A helium-4 nucleus (two protons and two neutrons) emitted from an unstable nucleus
The region on a plot of neutron number against proton number containing the stable nuclides
The decay of a proton in the nucleus into a neutron, a positron (emitted) and an electron neutrino
items.answer: The decay of a proton in the nucleus into a neutron, a positron (emitted) and an electron neutrino
items.markingKey: D. "beta-plus decay" is the decay of a proton in the nucleus into a neutron, a positron (emitted) and an electron neutrino.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The property that it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability of decay in a given time"?
items.answer: random decay
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of random decay.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The difference between the total mass of the separated nucleons and the mass of the nucleus"?
items.answer: mass defect
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of mass defect.

items.stem: Light stable nuclei have N ≈ Z, but heavy stable nuclei have N > Z. This is mainly because
options: electric repulsion between protons grows faster with Z than the strong attraction
items.answer: electric repulsion between protons grows faster with Z than the strong attraction
items.markingKey: D. Coulomb energy ∝ Z².

items.stem: In a cloud chamber, alpha tracks are
items.answer: short, thick and straight
items.markingKey: C. Heavy, strongly ionising particles travel straight and stop quickly.

items.stem: Isabel is revising alpha, beta and gamma decay and nuclear equations. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Uranium-238 is more stable than iron-56 because it has a larger total binding energy.
Gamma emission does not change Z or A; the element is unchanged.
Background radiation comes mainly from nuclear power stations.
In alpha decay the nucleon number decreases by 2.
items.answer: Gamma emission does not change Z or A; the element is unchanged.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Gamma emission does not change Z or A; the element is unchanged.

items.stem: Explain the difference between count rate and activity.
items.answer: Activity is the actual number of decays per second in the source; count rate is the number detected per second, which is smaller because the detector intercepts only some radiation and includes background.
items.markingKey: Activity is the actual number of decays per second in the source; count rate is the number detected per second, which is smaller because the detector intercepts only some radiation and includes background. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Uranium-238 is more stable than iron-56 because it has a larger total binding energy." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon: Fe-56 ≈ 8.8 MeV vs U-238 ≈ 7.6 MeV.
items.markingKey: Stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon: Fe-56 ≈ 8.8 MeV vs U-238 ≈ 7.6 MeV. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the strong nuclear force and the electromagnetic force.
items.answer: The strong force is very strong, attractive between all nucleons, short-range (~fm) and charge-independent; the electromagnetic force is weaker at nuclear distances, acts only between charges, can repel and has infinite range.
items.markingKey: The strong force is very strong, attractive between all nucleons, short-range (~fm) and charge-independent; the electromagnetic force is weaker at nuclear distances, acts only between charges, can repel and has infinite range. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The half-value thickness of lead for a gamma source is 1.0 cm. What percentage of the gamma rays pass through 4.0 cm of lead?
items.markingKey: D. 4 half-value thicknesses: 100 %/2^4 = 6.25 %.

items.stem: "Gamma decay changes the element." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Gamma emission does not change Z or A; the element is unchanged.
items.markingKey: Gamma emission does not change Z or A; the element is unchanged. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]

items.stem: The binding energy per nucleon of ⁶²Ni (Z = 28) is 8.795 MeV. What is its total binding energy?
items.markingKey: C. E_B = A × (E_B/A) = 62 × 8.795 = 545 MeV; multiplying by Z or N is a common error.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "The strong force holds electrons in their orbits." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Electrons are bound by the electromagnetic force; the strong force does not act on electrons (leptons).
items.markingKey: Electrons are bound by the electromagnetic force; the strong force does not act on electrons (leptons). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Background radiation comes mainly from nuclear power stations." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Nuclear power contributes a tiny fraction (<0.1 %); radon, rocks, cosmic rays, food and medical uses dominate.
items.markingKey: Nuclear power contributes a tiny fraction (<0.1 %); radon, rocks, cosmic rays, food and medical uses dominate. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A nucleus decays to ¹⁵N (Z = 7) by β⁺ emission. Identify the parent nucleus (proton number and nucleon number).
items.markingKey: Reverse the changes for β⁺ decay (M1): Z = 8, A = 15, i.e. O-15 (A1).

items.stem: Deuterium (²H, nuclear mass 2.013553 u) can be split into a proton and a neutron by a gamma photon (photodisintegration). (a) Calculate the binding energy of the deuteron. (b) Determine the minimum photon frequency needed. (c) Explain why in practice a slightly larger photon energy is needed (consider momentum).
items.answer: (a) Δm = 1.007276 + 1.008665 − 2.013553 = 0.002388 u; E_B = 2.22 MeV; (b) f = E/h = 2.22 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5.4 × 10²⁰ Hz; (c) the photon carries momentum, so the products must move, requiring extra kinetic energy beyond E_B.
items.markingKey: (a) Δm = 1.007276 + 1.008665 − 2.013553 = 0.002388 u; E_B = 2.22 MeV; (b) f = E/h = 2.22 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5.4 × 10²⁰ Hz; (c) the photon carries momentum, so the products must move, requiring extra kinetic energy beyond E_B.

items.stem: Using a sketch of the N–Z plot of stable nuclides, discuss how the competition between the strong nuclear force and the electromagnetic force accounts for (a) the shape of the band of stability, (b) the existence of alpha decay, and (c) the decay modes of nuclides on either side of the band.
items.answer: (a) For low Z the band follows N = Z; as Z increases it curves above the line (N/Z ≈ 1.5 at Pb) because extra neutrons supply strong attraction without Coulomb repulsion; the band ends near Z = 83. (b) In heavy nuclei Coulomb repulsion makes emission of a tightly bound α particle energetically favourable, reducing Z and A together. (c) Above the band (neutron-rich) β⁻ converts n → p; below (proton-rich) β⁺ or electron capture converts p → n; both are weak-force processes moving the nuclide towards the band.
items.markingKey: Correct sketch and N = Z line (A1); explanation of curvature (R1); end of the band and alpha decay (R1); β⁻ and β⁺ regions (R1 R1); role of weak force (A1).

items.stem: Design an experiment to show that gamma radiation obeys an inverse-square law, using a Geiger–Müller tube and counter. Include how you would deal with background radiation, the random nature of decay and the unknown position of the effective detection point in the tube.
items.answer: Measure background for 10 min. Measure counts over a fixed time at several distances d from a ruler mark, repeating each; subtract background. Since C = k/(d + e)², plot 1/√C against d: a straight line confirms the law and the x-intercept gives −e (the offset of the detection point). Use long counting times (N > 1000) to reduce the relative uncertainty (≈ 1/√N), handle the source with tongs, keep distance, minimise exposure time.
items.markingKey: Background measured and subtracted (A1); range of distances and repeat counts (A1); linearisation 1/√C vs d (M1 A1); random uncertainty ∝ √N addressed (R1); safety (R1).

items.stem: In β⁻ decay, which particles are emitted?
options: an electron and an electron antineutrino
a helium nucleus and a photon
items.answer: an electron and an electron antineutrino
items.markingKey: B. n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.

items.stem: After three half-lives, the fraction of the original nuclei remaining is
Which of the following best describes "unified atomic mass unit"?
options: One-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻²
The fundamental interaction responsible for beta decay, which changes the flavour of quarks
The ability of radiation to pass through matter before being absorbed
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, producing ions
items.answer: One-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻²
items.markingKey: A. "unified atomic mass unit" is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻².

items.stem: Arjun and a classmate in Kuala Lumpur disagree about fundamental forces and the stability of nuclei. Which statement is correct?
options: The half-life is half the time it takes for the whole sample to decay.
Gamma rays are completely stopped by a thin sheet of lead.
Neutrons are uncharged; they are held by the strong nuclear force.
Neutrons are held in the nucleus by electric attraction to protons.
items.answer: Neutrons are uncharged; they are held by the strong nuclear force.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. Neutrons are uncharged; they are held by the strong nuclear force.

items.stem: Explain why gamma radiation intensity decreases with distance from a point source even in air.
items.answer: Gamma rays spread out in all directions, so the intensity follows an inverse-square law (I ∝ 1/r²); absorption in air is very small.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gamma rays spread out in all directions, so the intensity follows an inverse-square law (I ∝ 1/r²); absorption in air is very small. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which quark change occurs in β⁻ decay?
options: a down quark changes to an up quark
an up quark changes to a down quark
a strange quark changes to an up quark
items.answer: a down quark changes to an up quark
items.markingKey: B. udd (n) → uud (p).

items.stem: A graph of ln(activity) against time for a pure radioisotope is
options: a straight line through the origin
items.answer: a straight line of gradient −λ
items.markingKey: A. ln A = ln A₀ − λt.

items.stem: Tomás writes four statements while revising mass defect, binding energy and binding energy per nucleon. Which one is a misconception?
options: Binding energy is the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart; it is released when the nucleus forms, so bound nuclei have LESS energy (mass) than free nucleons.
Neutrons are uncharged; they are held by the strong nuclear force.
It decreases by 4 (two protons and two neutrons); the proton number decreases by 2.
Uranium-238 is more stable than iron-56 because it has a larger total binding energy.
items.answer: Uranium-238 is more stable than iron-56 because it has a larger total binding energy.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon: Fe-56 ≈ 8.8 MeV vs U-238 ≈ 7.6 MeV.

items.stem: Which exchange particle mediates the weak interaction?
items.answer: W and Z bosons
items.markingKey: A. W± and Z⁰.

items.stem: A student measures the count rate (counts per minute) from a source with different absorbers: no absorber 636; paper 636; 5 mm aluminium 286; 5 cm lead 61. The background count rate is 36 counts per minute. Identify the radiation(s) emitted and justify your answer.
items.answer: β and γ
items.markingKey: Drop with paper (636 → 636) is negligible, so no α (R1); drop with aluminium (636 → 286) shows β (R1); count after aluminium above background shows γ (R1); conclusion: β and γ (A1).

items.stem: A nucleus decays to ²³⁵U (Z = 92) by α emission. Identify the parent nucleus (proton number and nucleon number).
items.markingKey: Reverse the changes for α decay (M1): Z = 94, A = 239, i.e. Pu-239 (A1).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "The half-life is half the time it takes for the whole sample to decay." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The whole sample never decays completely in a finite time; the half-life is the time for the number of nuclei to halve.
items.markingKey: The whole sample never decays completely in a finite time; the half-life is the time for the number of nuclei to halve. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The nuclear mass of ¹⁴¹Ba (Z = 56) is 140.883685 u. Calculate (a) its mass defect, (b) its binding energy in MeV, (c) its binding energy per nucleon. (mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u)
items.markingKey: Δm = 56mₚ + 85mₙ − m = 1.260296 u (M1 A1); E_B = Δm × 931.5 = 1174 MeV (A1); per nucleon 8.33 MeV (A1).

items.answer: α and γ
items.markingKey: Drop with paper (586 → 286) shows α (R1); drop with aluminium (286 → 286) is negligible, so no β (R1); count after aluminium above background shows γ (R1); conclusion: α and γ (A1).

items.stem: A decay chain starts at ²³⁵U (Z = 92) and ends at a nuclide with Z = 82 and A = 207. Determine the number of α and β⁻ decays in the chain.
items.answer: 7 α and 4 β⁻
items.markingKey: A changes only in α decay: (235 − 207)/4 = 7 α (M1 A1); Z: 92 − 2×7 + n_β = 82 → n_β = 4 (M1 A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Radiocarbon dating can be used to date any ancient object."
items.answer: Powerful but limited to organic materials younger than about 50 000 years, with calibration; other isotopes are needed for rocks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: excellent for organic material up to ~50 000 years; calibrated against tree rings. Arguments against: only for once-living material containing carbon; too few ¹⁴C nuclei remain after ~10 half-lives; atmospheric ¹⁴C levels have varied (calibration needed); contamination with modern carbon. Supported judgement: Powerful but limited to organic materials younger than about 50 000 years, with calibration; other isotopes are needed for rocks.

items.stem: Sketch the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number from A = 1 to 240 and use it to explain (a) why iron is the end product of fusion in massive stars, (b) why the energy per nucleon released in fusion of hydrogen is larger than in fission of uranium, and (c) why helium-4 lies above the general trend.
items.answer: Graph: rises steeply from 1.1 MeV (²H) with a spike at ⁴He (7.1 MeV), peaks at ~8.8 MeV near A = 56–62, then falls gradually to ~7.6 MeV at A = 238. (a) beyond iron, fusion lowers BE/A, so it absorbs energy and cannot sustain the star; (b) the curve is much steeper at low A, so the increase in BE/A in fusing hydrogen (~6–7 MeV per nucleon) far exceeds the ~0.8 MeV per nucleon gained in uranium fission; (c) ⁴He is an especially tightly bound arrangement of two protons and two neutrons.
items.markingKey: Correct sketch with values (A1 A1); iron argument (R1); steepness comparison (R1); He-4 explanation (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The strong nuclear force is the most important of the fundamental forces."
items.answer: Each force dominates at its own scale; "most important" depends on the phenomenon considered.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it binds nuclei and makes atoms and chemistry possible; it is the strongest at nuclear distances. Arguments against: gravity governs planets, stars and galaxies; electromagnetism governs chemistry and materials; the weak force drives stellar fusion (p → n). Supported judgement: Each force dominates at its own scale; "most important" depends on the phenomenon considered. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "Smoke detectors containing americium-241 are a safe use of radioactivity in the home." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Safe in normal use because alpha particles are contained; risks arise only from misuse or disposal.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Am-241 emits alpha particles that cannot penetrate the casing; activity is small (~37 kBq); saves many lives from fires. Arguments against: long half-life (432 y) needs careful disposal; danger if the source is removed and ingested. Supported judgement: Safe in normal use because alpha particles are contained; risks arise only from misuse or disposal. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
